opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the right answer is: not very confident. And I'd say that applies to me and to the projects I've supported as much as anyone else.

When I look at the history of people trying to shape the long-run future, a lot of it is a story of good intentions with ambiguous or even counterproductive results. With AI specifically, the situation is unusually murky. You can work on something that seems clearly helpful, say, advancing safety research or building up a lab that cares about doing things responsibly, and it's genuinely hard to rule out that you're also accelerating the overall pace of development, intensifying a race dynamic, or lending credibility to approaches that turn out to be wrong. A lot of the most important effects are second- and third-order, and those are exactly the ones we're worst at predicting.

So I tend to think about it less as "Is this project good?" with a confident yes or no, and more as "What's my best guess, how robust is it, and how would I find out if I'm wrong?" Some things seem more robustly positive than others. Trying to understand what's going on inside these systems, developing ways to evaluate whether a model has dangerous capabilities, helping governments and companies get better at noticing and reacting to warning signs: those strike me as fairly hard to make things worse with, though not impossible. Things that involve pushing capabilities forward, or big strategic bets about which actors should be in the lead, I'd hold with a lot more humility.

I don't think the conclusion is paralysis. If you think this could be one of the most important transitions in history, then sitting it out is also a choice with consequences. But I'd encourage people to hold their views loosely, to stay in touch with people who disagree with them, to be wary of the story where their own project is obviously the crucial one, and to keep asking whether the work would still look good if a few of their key assumptions turned out to be wrong. I think a healthy dose of "I might be making things worse here" is appropriate for basically everyone in this space.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is: not very confident, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who told you otherwise.

When I look at the history of people trying to do good for the long-run future, the track record is pretty humbling. Most of the big, deliberate attempts to steer the world in some direction either didn't matter much or had effects nobody anticipated. And AI is a particularly hard case because the thing we're trying to influence is, almost by definition, a technology whose consequences we don't understand yet. If we fully understood it, it wouldn't be the kind of transformative thing we're worried about.

So I'd break the question into two parts. One is: can you be confident that your specific project will help? And I think the answer there is usually no. If you're working on alignment research, or policy, or forecasting, or building safety culture at a lab, you should hold open the real possibility that your work ends up irrelevant, or gets used in ways you didn't intend, or that the whole framing you were operating under turns out to be wrong. I've been wrong about plenty of things in this space, and I expect to be wrong about more.

The other part is: can you be confident that the overall effort, the portfolio of people trying to make this go well, is better than nobody trying? And there I'm a lot more comfortable. It's a bit like asking whether you should bother wearing a seatbelt when you don't know if you'll crash. You don't need confidence that this particular drive is the one where it matters. You just need to think the expected value is clearly positive and the cost is reasonable.

What I'd push back on is the idea that uncertainty means you should do nothing, or that you should only act once you're sure. That standard would rule out basically every important thing anyone has ever done. The alternative to acting under uncertainty isn't acting under certainty. It's letting the outcome be decided by people who aren't thinking about it at all, or by default dynamics like competition and short-term incentives.

So my practical advice is: pick things that look robustly good across a lot of different scenarios, rather than things that only pay off if your particular model of the future is right. Keep your beliefs loosely held. Pay attention to feedback where you can get it, because a lot of this work has very long feedback loops and you can go years without learning whether you were right. And try to be the kind of person who updates visibly when the evidence comes in, because I think the community's ability to course-correct matters more than any individual bet being right.

I'd rather be in a world where a lot of thoughtful people are trying hard, being wrong a fair amount, and correcting, than one where everyone waited for confidence they were never going to get.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very hard to be confident about that. AI could have enormous benefits, but that doesn’t mean that any particular project that advances AI is making the long-run future better. You have to ask what you’re changing relative to what would have happened otherwise.

Are you helping us get powerful AI sooner? Are you helping us understand it better, control it better, or make better decisions about how to deploy it? Those can have very different implications. If you’re mostly accelerating capabilities, I don’t think you should take for granted that the benefits outweigh the risks.

That doesn’t mean you need certainty before doing anything. But I’d want a fairly concrete account of why your project helps, including what could go wrong and what evidence would change your mind. “AI will be useful, and I’m working on AI” isn’t enough to establish that.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should be pretty uncertain. There’s a big difference between being confident that AI will be enormously consequential and being confident that a particular project will make things go better. You can believe the first without believing the second.

If you’re making AI more capable, you might be helping us get to some really extraordinary benefits sooner. But you might also be shortening the time we have to figure out how to handle the risks. So I wouldn’t take “this advances AI” as sufficient reason to think a project is good for the long-run future.

I’d want to ask: What problem is this project solving? Why do we think that problem is a bottleneck to a good outcome? And what happens if the project succeeds—does it make powerful AI easier to understand and control, or does it mostly make it arrive sooner?

You’re not going to get certainty out of those questions. But I think you can get a much better basis for deciding what to work on than a general sense that technological progress is good.
